How to See the Northern Lights This Winter

By EarthLive.TV | Published 17 August 2026
In this article
  1. Where the Light Actually Comes From
  2. Why 2026 Is Great
  3. Where to Stand
  4. Common Questions

On a clear night above the Arctic Circle, the sky sometimes stops behaving like a sky. Curtains of green rise out of the horizon, fold, brighten, and drift sideways at speeds that feel far too fast for something that large. EarthLive.TV keeps a set of live aurora cameras running through the northern winter, so you can check the sky without leaving the sofa.

The northern lights have been explained as dragons, as reflections off the polar ice, and as the spirits of the dead. The real answer is stranger than most of them: what you are watching is the Earth's magnetic field catching a stream of charged particles thrown off the surface of the Sun, and cashing them in as light.

Where the Light Actually Comes From

The Sun is constantly leaking. A thin stream of electrons and protons, the solar wind, pours outward in every direction at roughly 400 kilometres per second. Most of it misses us. What does reach Earth runs into the magnetosphere, the magnetic bubble our planet's molten iron core generates around itself.

That bubble deflects almost everything. But at the poles, the field lines bend inward and funnel particles down into the upper atmosphere. Around 100 to 300 kilometres up, those particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms, knock their electrons into a higher energy state, and light is released when the electrons drop back down.

The colour tells you the altitude and the gas. Green, by far the most common, is oxygen at around 100 to 250 kilometres. Red is oxygen higher up, above 250 kilometres, where the air is thin enough for the slower red emission to complete. Blue and violet are nitrogen, and usually appear along the lower edge of a bright display. The same physics lights up the southern sky as the aurora australis, which you can read about in our guide to Earth's four most extreme live cameras.

What each colour tells you
ColourGasAltitudeHow often
GreenOxygen100–250 kmAlmost every display
RedOxygenAbove 250 kmStrong storms only
BlueNitrogenBelow 100 kmLower edge of bright arcs
VioletNitrogenBelow 100 kmRare, needs a dark sky

You are not watching weather. You are watching the Sun, arriving late.

Why 2026 Is Great

The Sun runs on an eleven-year cycle of magnetic activity. At solar minimum its face is nearly blank. At solar maximum it is covered in sunspots, and the coronal mass ejections that produce the strongest auroras become routine rather than rare.

We are currently on the declining side of Solar Cycle 25, which peaked in 2024. That sounds like bad news, but it is not. The years just after a solar maximum reliably produce some of the strongest geomagnetic storms of the entire cycle, because the Sun's field is at its most tangled. The displays that reach as far south as the United Kingdom and the northern United States tend to arrive now, not at the peak.

Reading the forecast

Aurora forecasting is measured on the Kp index, a nine-point scale of geomagnetic disturbance. The useful thing to understand is the delay: a coronal mass ejection takes between one and three days to cross the distance from the Sun. That is your warning window, and it is why aurora forecasts are unusually reliable compared with ordinary weather.

If you would rather watch something that erupts on a shorter fuse, our volcano cameras need no forecast at all.

How far south each Kp level reaches

4Reykjavík, YellowknifeClear movement, good photographs
5Scotland, northern statesOverhead bands, visible to the naked eye
7London, New YorkThe kind people post about

    Where to Stand

    The aurora does not appear directly above the North Pole. It forms an oval roughly centred on the magnetic pole, which means the best viewing sits in a band between about 65 and 72 degrees north. Go further north than that and you can end up inside the ring, looking at empty sky.

    Tromsø, Norway sits almost perfectly on the oval and has an airport, which makes it the least difficult option. Abisko, Sweden has a rain shadow that gives it more clear nights than anywhere else in Scandinavia. Fairbanks, Alaska is inland and dry, with 200-plus aurora nights a year, and sits close enough to the Alaskan wildlife cameras to make a trip worth doubling up. Iceland is easy to reach but cloudy, so build in extra days.

    Timelapse
    Timelapse · 4 hours

    Four hours of sky compressed into a few seconds. The stars appear to rotate because the Earth does, and the still point is roughly where Polaris sits.

    Three practical things nobody tells you. The season runs from late September to late March, because you need genuine darkness rather than cold. Full moons wash out weak displays, so check the lunar calendar before booking.

    Our full camera directory lists what is live tonight, wherever you end up. And your camera will always see more colour than your eyes do, because human night vision is nearly monochrome. A display that looks pale grey to you can come out vividly green on the sensor.

    Which is worth knowing before you stand outside at minus twenty for four hours, feeling faintly disappointed by something genuinely extraordinary.

    Common questions
    When is the best time of year to see the northern lights?

    Late September to late March. You need genuine darkness rather than cold, so the limiting factor is daylight hours, not temperature. Between May and August the midnight sun makes viewing impossible across most of the auroral zone, which is also why most aurora webcams go offline over the summer.

    Do I need a Kp index of 5 or higher?

    Not if you are inside the auroral oval. From Tromsø or Fairbanks a Kp of 3 will show you something. Kp 5 is the threshold for Scotland and the northern United States, and Kp 7 is roughly when London and New York start seeing it.

    Why does the aurora look grey to my eyes but green in photographs?

    Human night vision is nearly monochrome. The rod cells that work in low light don't carry colour information, so a faint display reads as pale grey. A camera sensor has no such limitation and records the green at full saturation.

    Can you see the northern lights from a plane?

    Yes, and often better than from the ground, because you are above the cloud. Ask for a window seat on the north-facing side and turn the cabin light off. Transatlantic routes between Europe and the west coast of North America cross high enough latitudes to work.

    How far in advance can an aurora be forecast?

    One to three days. That is how long a coronal mass ejection takes to travel from the Sun to Earth, which makes aurora forecasting considerably more reliable than ordinary weather forecasting over the same window.
